devpost_page.title: Pyrosense
devpost_page.tagline: a wearable live hazard map that builds itself as you walk

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Firefighters entering unfamiliar buildings have to make critical decisions. This necessitates situational awareness, but enter smoke, heat, darkness, and changing airflow, and it becomes difficult to understand both the structure and how hazardous gases are distributed inside it. Many dangerous gases (VOCs) are invisible and cannot be reliably detected by humans without sensors. Existing gas monitors are essential, but they still rely heavily on manual sampling. Firefighters may need to take readings at multiple locations because concentration can change with airflow, ventilation, vapor density, and sensor response time. These readings are collected at different places and times and thrown away rather than forming one continuous view. As a result, individual measurements may only be seen by the firefighter carrying the monitor or relayed verbally to command. This makes it difficult for the whole team to maintain a unified understanding of where hazards are concentrated, how conditions are changing, and which areas remain unmeasured. GPS is also unreliable indoors, and building plans may be missing, outdated, or incomplete.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Our system creates one live spatial view of hazards (past, present, and predicted future) inside an unfamiliar building. The view maps indoor layout, firefighter locations, and gas concentrations. It starts with the firefighter’s helmet . A compact sensing unit is mounted on the helmet. As it moves with them through the structure, it generates a structural map, tracks their position, and links gas readings to where they were collected. These readings form a live gas concentration heat map that highlights hazardous areas, shows changing conditions, and identifies unsampled regions, displayed onto the dashboard for the incident commander or chief on site. The system also visually and audibly alerts firefighters to dangerous conditions such as rapidly rising gas levels or entry into high hazard areas. The incident commander, who coordinates crews and tactical decisions, can add reported information such as victims, blocked exits, entry points, and other hazards directly onto the map. The system must fit into existing fireground workflows. Firefighting procedures with PyroSense keep radio communication and command procedures in place. PyroSense automatically adds mapping and environmental data to tablets or laptops already used for coordination by chiefs and incidence commanders.

sections.heading: Hardware design
sections.text: The wearable prototype is built around a Raspberry Pi 5, which collects and synchronizes data from each sensor. A LiDAR sensor continuously scans the surroundings to generate the building layout and support indoor localization. An IMU measures motion and tilt to help track the orientation of the mapping system and reject unreliable LiDAR scans when the sensor is tilted too far. For environmental sensing, we use a volatile organic compounds (VOC) sensor to continuously measure relative VOC levels. The Raspberry Pi then streams the sensor data to a laptop, where the mapping, hazard visualization, and command interface are processed and displayed.

sections.heading: Software architecture
sections.text: For deployment, we run backend and dashboard on a single Vultr VM with Docker Compose. FastAPI pulls the Pi's stream over Tailscale, and nginx serves the dashboard. Readings go to Tiger Cloud, which turns them into the heat map, so replaying a past walk is just a time-range query. One script deploys everything. Dashboard was made possible with three.js. We render walls from the SLAM map as it fills in, paint the gas field on the floor, and draw the air above it as drifting particles. You can watch from overhead or drop into first person at the firefighter's eye height, looking where they look as they move. Incident command gets layer toggles, follow mode, per-responder exposure history, and one-click marks for victims, fire and blocked exits. Also made a really cool landing page!

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Hardware bring up: Debugging drivers, SSH, and hotspot issues to connect our Raspberry Pi to our laptop. Data streaming latency: Reduced Pi to frontend latency by 50% by transmitting only new sensor readings, cutting traffic by about 10×, lowering SLAM map update frequency, serving live data from memory, and sending map images only when they changed. Data visualization: Designing an intuitive way to display the building map, gas heat map, changing conditions, and unsampled areas.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Full complete prototype: We successfully integrated mapping, localization, and gas sensing into a wearable solution that works in real-time. Hazard mapping and prediction: Used Gaussian Processing to produce accurate gas maps with Good workflow integration: We made sure that our solution integrates seamlessly into existing workflows so that firefighters can adopt it easily!

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: When doing Raspberry Pi setup without a monitor, make sure to install Ubuntu server and not desktop!

sections.heading: What's next for Pyrosense
sections.text: Next, we want to adapt the prototype for real fireground conditions. A key next step is replacing optical LiDAR with mmWave radar , which can continue mapping through dense smoke, darkness, and dust where cameras and optical LiDAR struggle. Thermal imaging could also be fused with radar to improve visibility and detect heat sources. We also plan to integrate certified gas sensors, SCBA air and emergency status, and further tune gas source estimation and short term hazard prediction using real-world data. The next major step would be testing the system with firefighters and fire departments to gather feedback, validate its usefulness in real scenarios, and eventually bring it to market.

devpost_page.title: On Your Terms
devpost_page.tagline: Ever wondered how easy would it be if we could get a summary of long page terms and conditions on our favorite website. Wonder no more, you have AI solution 'On Your Terms'.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: When was the last time you read any terms of service or policy document? It is a guaranteed answer: never. A 2019 Pew Research Center study found that only 9% of U.S. adults say they "always" read a company's privacy policy before agreeing to it. Unknowingly, we give access to all our data, our pictures, and whatever we share online to the big companies. If there is any misuse or data breach online, we no longer hold any right to bring companies to court because we chose to skip reading through the terms and conditions, as it was too long for our eyes. Plagued by the problem of not encouraging ourselves to go through the lengthy lines of terms and rules, we decided to make a creative solution to ease the discomfort of looking through long pages of company policies. You can easily summarize the details of the terms and sign the policies On Your Terms

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: On Your Terms gives you a summarized view of companies' policies of data use and ranks the seriousness of the contract(s) with the score associated with them. This tool sits on your browser as an extension, scanning and flagging any hyperlinks containing company policy and terms. The tool analyzes the hidden contract terms in the background and assigns a score on how seriously you need to take the terms while committing to them. Don't worry if the contract document has a seriously low score ; you don't need to go through a 10-page-long contract. The tool also highlights the major points that need consideration on the side window. On Your Terms takes full care of its users by providing one-on-one chat to further explain policy points where you need more assistance understanding the terms.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We automated the whole process of scanning the website, flagging the hyperlinks, analyzing the terms, and providing chat assistance with the n8n workflow automation tool in the background. The browser extension built on manifest.json sits at the frontend, scanning and interacting with the user on chat, while the automation workflow sits at the backend, acting on trigger events to parse data from the frontend, storing it in a database, passing back the score to the frontend, allowing the user to interact with NVIDIA's Nemotron agentic AI if the user chooses to. We had a seamless integration of a browser extension, a safe database, and a robust AI chatbot using LangChain, solving the tedious task of reading terms and conditions in minutes instead of hours.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: It was our first time working with a browser extension, n8n automation workflow, and LangChain. We encountered errors with data mismatch while implementing these tools, but they weren't that tough to handle. We had major trouble working with the browser extension. Since the browser extension doesn't allow the use of a library like Selenium to scrape the data on the website in the background, we spent a long time before we were able to scrape and send the scraped data to the endpoint. We had another big trouble routing the scraped data to the LangChain. We faced some trouble while integrating all the tools on the n8n automation tool as well, due to differences in the expected and delivered data types. We were able to tackle all the errors with localized debugging and gradually integrate the whole tool chains to put a robust model.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are proud that we were able to solve the problem we face every day, but we casually choose to ignore it. We couldn't think of a better use of AI than to make tedious tasks easier and prevent everyone from silent privacy invasion. Making a fully working system that brings different tech into a single automated integration to tackle a normal person faces on a daily basis is what we expected to gain from this hackathon. Besides, we also got to learn so many new tools like LangChain, n8n automation, and building a browser extension. Overall, it has been a 10/10 project based on the complexity of the problem statement, impact on daily life, and learning outcomes.

We wanted to answer the question: "Can we see how network outages and poor 5G quality directly impact customer happiness?" We set out to build a tool that would correlate live social media sentiment and a "Customer Happiness Index" (CHI) with real-time network performance data.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: MagentaMonitor is a real-time dashboard that provides a comprehensive overview of customer sentiment and its relationship to network quality. Its key features include: KPI Dashboard: At-a-glance metrics for the overall Customer Happiness Index (CHI), live sentiment (which blinks red when "Very Unhappy"), total posts analyzed, and average 5G quality. Live Sentiment vs. CHI: A time-series chart that plots live positive, negative, and neutral sentiment from Reddit directly against the calculated CHI score, complete with a "live update" pulse animation. Network Quality & Outages: A time-series chart that tracks 5G, Wireless, and Cellular quality over time, overlaying reported outages as red bars. Interactive CHI Predictor: A "what-if" tool that allows a user to adjust sliders for network quality (5G, Wireless, Cellular) and toggle reported outages, then submit those inputs to a (simulated) API to get a predicted CHI score. Correlation Scatter Plot: An interactive chart plotting CHI vs. 5G Quality to visualize their correlation. Clicking on any month's dot (colored red for outages) instantly filters the post table to show data for that specific month. Live Post Table: A filterable table showing the most recent, relevant posts from Reddit, which updates based on selections from the scatter plot. Sentiment Breakdowns: Pie charts and bar charts that show the distribution of happiness levels (Happy, Unhappy, etc.) and the top sources of Reddit discussion.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: MagentaMonitor is a single-page application built entirely in React . Frontend: We used React with functional components and hooks ( useState , useEffect , useMemo ). Data Visualization: All charts were custom-built using the Recharts library, including LineChart , ComposedChart , BarChart , PieChart , and ScatterChart . Data Handling: Data is currently loaded from static JSON files ( customer_happiness_index.json , reddit_data.json , network_data...json ). We use useEffect to fetch this data on load and setInterval to re-fetch every 10 seconds, creating a "live" update illusion. Prediction Model: The scatter plot's trend line and the CHI predictor's score are calculated using a simple linear regression model we built in JavaScript to find the correlation between 5G quality and CHI. Styling: All styling was done from scratch using CSS , including a dark mode theme, responsive grid layouts, and custom @keyframes animations for the blinking KPI, pulsing "live" indicators, and chart update glows.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: We encountered several challenges along the way: Data Integration: Merging three different JSON sources (CHI, Reddit, Network) that shared a date key was a primary challenge. We solved this using useEffect to process the data and useMemo to create combined datasets for the charts. Layout & Responsiveness: We iterated on the layout multiple times, moving from a simple 2x2 grid to a complex layout with a vertical sidebar. This required significant adjustments to our CSS grid and component structure. Debugging: We ran into "Failed to load data" errors, which we traced back to a simple typo in a JSON filename ( netowrk vs. network ). Interactivity: Implementing the scatter-plot-to-table filter was complex. It required managing a new state for the selectedMonth , adding click handlers to the scatter plot, and writing filter logic to update the filteredRedditPosts state. Simulating an API: Building the predictor required us to refactor our code, changing it from a live-updating calculation ( useEffect ) to a button-click ( onSubmit ) model that simulates an API call with async/await and a setTimeout .

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are particularly proud of the features that make the dashboard feel dynamic and interactive: The CHI Predictor: Building the full UI for the predictor and wiring up the "Run Prediction" button to a simulated API call and a real regression model was a huge success. The Interactive Scatter Plot: The "click-to-filter" functionality that links the correlation chart directly to the Reddit post table is a powerful analysis tool. The "Live" Illusions: We successfully used setInterval , CSS animations ( @keyframes ), and state triggers ( isPulsing ) to make the dashboard feel alive, with blinking KPIs and pulsing charts that glow on data refresh.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Power of Correlation: We learned how to visually and programmatically connect two seemingly different datasets (customer feelings and network stats) to find a real correlation. React Hooks for Data: We gained a deep understanding of how to use useState , useEffect , and useMemo to fetch, process, merge, and display complex data from multiple sources. Advanced Recharts: We went beyond simple line charts to implement complex ComposedChart s, interactive ScatterChart s with trend lines, and custom-styled PieChart s. CSS Animations: We learned how to use @keyframes to create dynamic UI elements like blinking, pulsing, and glowing effects that significantly improve the user experience.

sections.heading: What's next for MagentaMonitor
sections.text: The current version is a powerful, data-driven prototype. The next logical steps are: Connect to a Real ML Model: Replace our simple linear regression with a fetch call to a real, Python-based machine learning model (e.g., in a Flask/FastAPI backend) that can run a multi-variable prediction using all the slider inputs. Connect to Live Data Streams: Replace the static JSON files with calls to live APIs. This would mean polling a live network monitoring endpoint and streaming data from the Reddit API to make the dashboard truly "real-time." Enhance the Predictor: Use the outage toggle and other sliders (Wireless, Cellular) as inputs in the real prediction mod

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: For five years I worked as a tutor, and over that time I worked with many students with special needs. I also got to know their parents, several of whom worked as instructional assistants (IAs) in schools. Those conversations stayed with me. They described a community that is deeply committed but often stretched thin: students who get overwhelmed in the middle of a lesson and can’t always find the words to say so, and adults who are trying to notice and respond to many needs at once. They also described how hard it can be to keep strategies consistent between home and school. What stood out most was that none of this came from a lack of care. The families and educators I spoke with cared enormously. What was missing were tools that fit the moment, ones that are personal to each student, discreet, and respectful of their dignity. We chose techniques with real support behind them, like slow breathing and predictable routines, and we made privacy and sensory safety central to the design. I wanted to take action instead of only hearing about the problem. Ebb is our first step toward a solution that is built w

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Ebb is a smartwatch, an iPhone app and a website that help kids with special needs calm down before a meltdown, and keep their parents and teachers informed. On the watch Senses rising stress: it reads movement (rocking, hand-flapping) and room loudness, and compares them with what’s normal for this child. It keeps loudness levels only, never audio. Responds in steps: a gentle breathing buzz → a full calm mode (a breathing circle, a calm scene, a soothing voice, light vibration) → a “needs an adult” alert if it doesn’t settle. Starts calm three ways: by itself, when the child taps the watch, or when a teacher or parent taps Start in the app. Asks the child afterwards: three faces for better, same or worse. It learns Measures results: how much agitation dropped and how fast the child settled. Tunes itself: “False alarm” or “Helped” ratings from teachers make it less or more sensitive. Picks scenes: it learns which scene helps this child most at each time of day, and still tries new ones sometimes. Predicts: it forecasts the riskiest hours ahead. For the adults Parent setup: pair the watch with a QR code; fill in an assessment, and AI drafts a calm profile; choose the calm voice (an AI voice or their own cloned voice); approve 6 scenes each week. Teacher tools: start or stop calm, rate each moment, write journal notes. Live view and insights: a live agitation graph, a heatmap of when hard moments happen, what works, and an AI weekly report. Texting: parents and teachers can tex

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We got a programmable watch, created a ui for the website, app and watch. Connected the backend and the logins. We used photon for the messaging system. We used gemini for the profile for the assessment for the student done by the parent. We used the Arduino ide to push all the updates to the watch. We also used elevenlabs for the voice feature and voice cloning for the familiar parent/guardian.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: We definitely ran into lots of problems especially connecting the database to the watch, and making the watch usable.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A closed loop on real hardware. The watch senses rising agitation, buzzes a breathing cue, and starts calm mode by itself. It then measures whether the calm moment actually helped and feeds that back into its own settings. We tested this end to end on a LilyGO T-Watch S3 Plus. It learns per child. Its reward combines the teacher’s rating, the child’s own check-in, and the measured drop in agitation. A full product in one weekend: firmware; an iPhone app (QR pairing, live graphs, insights, location); a Supabase backend with row-level security on every table; a website; AI calm profiles and weekly reports; a calm voice that can be the parent’s own; iMessage texting for parents and teachers. Privacy from the start. Children are known by nickname only. The watch never records audio. Names are stripped before anything reaches the AI. Location is opt-in, and teachers can only see it during school hours. Old data is deleted automatically. We also fixed every issue our security reviews found before demo day.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Hardware is humbling. HTTPS failed until the watch synced its clock. Venue Wi-Fi was 5 GHz only, and the watch needs 2.4 GHz. A volume setting silently wrapped around to zero. The tiny speaker sets a hard ceiling on volume. Simple statistics carry a lot of weight. Defaults matter for kids. Auto-start is off until a parent turns it on, and adults always keep control. Security reviews catch real bugs. Ours found that an email-style iMessage handle could pose as a parent, and that a teacher could switch off auto-start by flipping “false alarm” on and off. Both are fixed. Integrations shape architecture. Photon’s iMessage connection needs a constantly running program, so we built a small bridge with a message outbox instead of forcing it into serverless functions.

sections.heading: What's next for Ebb
sections.text: Pilot with real classrooms and calibrate the agitation model with special-education teachers, behaviour analysts and occupational therapists. Add heart rate and skin response on future hardware for earlier, more accurate warnings, plus a louder speaker. Report against IEP goals so progress data supports each student’s individualized education plan. Become compliant: FERPA and COPPA review; school data agreements; deleting a child’s data with one tap; encrypted offline storage. Build an Android app and multi-classroom dashboards for schools. Train an on-device model on labelled moments, so the watch spots patterns before the numbers rise.

devpost_page.title: Synesthesia
devpost_page.tagline: Visualization of sound in augmented reality to assist the deaf and hard of hearing.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We were inspired by Minecraft’s Sound Subtitles and many video games’ visual sound effects, which show players where important sounds are coming from through on-screen indicators. We realized that this same idea could be used outside gaming to help people who are Deaf or hard of hearing understand the sounds happening around them, and stay more connected to the people they are with.

sections.heading: What We Built
sections.text: Synesthesia is a prototype AR-style sound-awareness system that helps users “see” nearby sound. A siren can appear as a red-and-blue alert on the side it came from, a knock can become a focused pulse in front of the wearer, and a person saying a saved name can trigger a clear visual notification and vibration. By turning sounds into visual, spatial cues, Synesthesia can help users notice when someone is trying to get their attention and participate more confidently in conversations, homes, classrooms, and social spaces.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.text: A Raspberry Pi Pico reads three microphone channels and estimates the rough direction of a sound based on relative sound levels. An optional rear-facing sensor provides an additional warning for sounds that may be behind the user. The Pico sends direction events over UART to an ESP32, which forwards them to the phone through Bluetooth Low Energy. On the phone, the web app uses the device microphone and an on-device YAMNet audio-classification model to recognize sounds such as alarms, sirens, horns, knocks, speech, dogs, doorbells, and more. The app pairs the recognized sound with a nearby direction event and displays an animated visual cue using color, shape, iconography, and motion. Users can also save their name and nicknames. Where supported, local speech recognition detects them and creates a more personal alert. The phone camera can provide a live background, creating an AR-style overlay that places sound cues into the user’s view of the real world.

sections.heading: Why AI Is Essential
sections.text: AI transforms raw sound into useful meaning. A simple volume sensor could show that something happened, but it could not distinguish a car horn from a knock, recognize speech, or identify when someone says the user’s name. Synesthesia uses on-device AI sound classification and local speech recognition to turn nearby audio into context-aware visual alerts. This is what makes the system useful for both safety awareness and everyday human connection.

sections.heading: Privacy
sections.text: Privacy was a major design goal. Audio is not transmitted over Bluetooth or uploaded to a server. The ESP32 sends only small direction packets, while sound classification and supported name recognition run locally on the phone.

sections.heading: Challenges We Faced
sections.text: The largest challenge was direction detection. The Pico does not perform true audio triangulation; it compares microphone loudness. This can be affected by echoes, microphone gain differences, distance, overlapping sounds, and background noise. To make the system more honest and useful, we added ambient-noise calibration, event thresholds, clipping detection, an ambiguity score, and a rear-only warning mode. When the system is unsure, it avoids claiming an exact direction. Another challenge was combining the sensor’s direction event with the phone’s sound classification. They do not share a clock, and multiple sounds can happen at once. We built a timing-based fusion layer that assigns a direction only when there is a clear nearby match. Otherwise, the app still shows the sound type without presenting a potentially incorrect bearing.

sections.heading: What We Learned
sections.text: Through this project, we learned about MicroPython firmware, analog microphone sensing, UART communication, Bluetooth Low Energy, browser hardware APIs, local machine-learning inference with MediaPipe and YAMNet, Canvas animation, and accessibility-focused interaction design. Most importantly, we learned that accessibility technology should communicate uncertainty clearly. Rather than treating every detection as certain, Synesthesia distinguishes between a confident cue, an unclear direction, and a possible sound behind the user.

sections.heading: Looking Forward
sections.text: Synesthesia is still a prototype, not a safety-certified navigation device. However, it demonstrates how a familiar idea from games can become a meaningful real-world accessibility tool. In the future, we hope to bring Synesthesia to AR glasses, using their microphones and displays to make sound awareness feel more immediate, immersive, and naturally integrated into everyday life.

sections.text: Sustain-ify is an app designed to empower people to make sustainable choices for the Earth and for themselves. It provides users with the tools to make sustainable choices in everyday life. The app focuses on dual sustainability—a future where both the Earth and its people thrive. Key features include: Eco Shopping Assistant : Guides users through eco-friendly shopping. DIY Assistant : Offers DIY sustainability projects. Health Reports : Helps users maintain a healthy lifestyle.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Sustain-ify was built with a range of technologies and frameworks to deliver a smooth, scalable, and user-friendly experience. Technical Architecture: Frontend Technologies: Frameworks: Flutter (Dart), Streamlit (Python) were used for the graphical user interface (GUI/front-end). Services in Future: Integration with third-party services such as Twilio, Lamini, and Firebase for added functionalities like messaging and real-time updates. Backend & Web Services: Node.js & Express.js: For the backend API services. FastAPI: RESTful API pipeline used for HTTP requests and responses. Appwrite: Backend server for authentication and user management. MongoDB Atlas: For storing pre-processed data chunks into a vector index. Data Processing & AI Models: ScrapeGraph.AI: LLM-powered web scraping framework used to extract structured data from online resources. Langchain & LlamaIndex: Used to preprocess scraped data and split it into chunks for efficient vector storage. BGE-Large Embedding Model: From Hugging Face, used for embedding textual content. Neo4j: For building a knowledge graph to improve data retrieval and structuring. Gemini gpt-40 & Groq: Large language models used for inference, running on LPUs (Language Processing Units) for a sustainable inference mechanism. Additional Services: Serper: Provides real-time data crawling and extraction from the internet, powered by LLMs that generate queries based on the user's input. Firebase: Used for storing and analyzing user-uploaded medic

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Throughout the development process, we faced several challenges: Ensuring data privacy and security during real-time data processing. Handling large amounts of scraped data from various online sources and organizing it for efficient querying and analysis. Scaling the inference mechanisms using LPUs to provide sustainable solutions without compromising performance.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We're proud of creating an app that: Addresses both environmental sustainability and personal well-being. Empowers people to make sustainable choices in their everyday lives. Provides practical tools like the Eco Shopping Assistant, DIY Assistant, and Health Reports. Has the potential to create a big impact through small, collective actions.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Through this project, we learned that: Sustainability isn't just about making eco-friendly choices; it's about making sustainable lifestyle choices too, focusing on personal health and well-being. Small, meaningful steps taken together can lead to a big impact. People have the power to change the world for the better, just as they have the power to impact it negatively.

sections.heading: What's next for Sustain-ify
sections.text: Moving forward, we aim to: Continue developing and refining our features to better serve our users. Expand our user base to increase our collective impact. Potentially add more features that address other aspects of sustainability. Work towards our vision of creating a sustainable future where both humans and the planet can flourish. Together, we believe we can create a sustainable future where both humans and the planet can thrive. That's the ongoing mission of Sustain-ify, and we're excited to continue bringing this vision to life!

sections.heading: Project details
sections.text: The Problem Every year, firefighters walk into buildings they've never seen. Search-and-rescue teams navigate rubble without a map. Visually impaired people enter new spaces with no spatial context. Emergency sweeps happen by memory and guesswork. AI could help if it could actually see. Today's AI agents are spatially blind. They process pixels and text, but have no concept of where things are in 3D space. Ask a state-of-the-art LLM "how many chairs are in this room?" while pointing a camera at it — and it will hallucinate an answer. It can describe what an object looks like, but not where it lives in space, how far away it is, or what's around the corner. The tools that do provide spatial maps, LiDAR rigs, depth cameras, survey hardware, cost tens of thousands of dollars and require trained operators. Spatial intelligence has stayed locked inside robotics labs. Open Reality breaks that barrier. What We Built Open Reality is a cloud-native spatial AI platform. Describe your task. Point a phone. An AI agent maps your space in real time, finds your targets, and answers spatial questions from any browser, from anywhere. The experience: Type your mission in plain English: "I'm a paramedic doing a safety sweep." Open Reality generates a spatial plan: what to look for, how to move through the space. Open the camera stream on your phone with a link. Walk the space. A 3D map builds live. The agent finds your targets automatically, pins them in 3D, and reasons & answers follow-up ques

devpost_page.title: Tempr
devpost_page.tagline: Music is the language of emotion and Tempr is the translator of that emotion. Through short form discovery, we gamify the process of discovering new music to break barriers between people and cultures

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We’ve all experienced Spotify Choice Paralysis , standing in a grocery store or sitting down for a long-work session, scrolling through hundreds of liked songs but finding nothing that fits the exact “vibe.” We built Tempr to bridge the gap between human emotion and digital libraries. Whether it’s a specific text prompt, a photo of a sunset, or an upcoming date on your calendar, Tempr ensures the user's life has a real-time, AI-generated soundtrack.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Tempr is an AI-powered music app that uses Gemini and Spotify to generate personalized music queues based on mood, vibe, and context. Users can describe how they feel or upload an image, and the app curates playlists directly from their liked songs. It also integrates with the device calendar to auto-generate playlists for upcoming events and sends notifications 10 minutes before they start. At a high level, we treat matching as a vector similarity search problem. We represent each track in a user’s library as an audio-feature embedding (using Spotify features like (acousticness), (danceability), (energy), and (valence)). Gemini then converts the user’s prompt (or image context) into a target vibe vector .We run a nearest-neighbor search over the library by computing cosine similarity between the target vector and each track vector, then select the top matches: $$ s_i = \cos(\theta) = \frac{\mathbf{v}\cdot \mathbf{x}_i}{|\mathbf{v}|\;|\mathbf{x}_i|} $$ $$ \text{TopTracks} = \operatorname*{argmax\,topK}_{i}\; s_i $$

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built Tempr as an Expo (React Native) app with TypeScript , and expo-router . Users log in with Spotify using Supabase Auth . We used the Gemini API to turn text prompts or images into queue suggestions, and the Spotify Web API to pull liked songs, match suggestions to real tracks, and add them to the playback queue. We also used 'Apple Calander' API to generate playlists for upcoming events and notify users 10 minutes before they start. For Discover, we use the YouTube Data API to show video previews.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The hardest part was reliability under real-world constraints: matching AI-generated song titles to the correct Spotify tracks, handling OAuth token expiry without breaking the session, and keeping the UI responsive during generation. Time vs. accuracy was a tradeoff we had to deal with because queue generation can take time (up to 30s), and searching a large liked library requires careful batching and caching. We solved this with batched Spotify searches, AsyncStorage caching for queues/likes/previews, strict formatting in Gemini prompts, and clear retry states when APIs fail.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A working end-to-end flow that goes from mood or image input to a playable Spotify queue. A calendar feature that generates playlists for upcoming events and notifies users before they start. A Memories library that saves queues and lets users re-add them to their Spotify queue with one tap. A Discover experience with swipe-to-like and YouTube previews that makes finding new music feel fast and fun.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned that the hardest part of an “AI app” isn’t the model. It’s everything around it: reliable auth, token refresh, caching, retries, and a UX that still feels trustworthy when APIs fail. We also learned that grounding generation in a user’s liked songs improves relevance, and that the biggest skill gain was API integration , wiring together Gemini, Spotify, Supabase Auth, calendar, and notifications while handling auth, rate limits, errors, and token refresh reliably.

sections.heading: What's next for Tempr
sections.text: Next, we want to add Group Vibes so multiple users can merge their liked libraries for shared events. We also plan to improve personalization with stronger matching confidence and lightweight feedback loops from likes/skips. Longer term, we want to incorporate real-time context signals (like location or biometric data such as heart rate during workouts) to automatically adjust queue energy as the user’s situation changes.
